title: Prophecy needs preparation
hook: prophecy requires mind, character and imagination

segments.voice: Yesterday, the strong hand as a picture of God's power, and the Raavad defending the plain reader. Your line: the hand is a metaphor. Today, a prophet who asks for music.

Three kings and their armies are stuck in a desert with no water, and they come to the prophet Elisha for a word from God. He has hard words for one of them, the king of Israel. Then he asks for something odd. Not a scroll, not an altar. A musician. "But now bring me a minstrel." The musician plays, and the text says the hand of the LORD came upon him, and he speaks. Why would a prophet need music first? Maimonides has an answer.
screen: `NO WATER IN THE DESERT.` → `ELISHA'S HARD WORDS.` → `BRING ME A MINSTREL.`

segments.voice: Prophecy needs preparation. First, the mind. In his law code, Maimonides writes that prophecy rests only on a person great in wisdom, strong in character, whose impulses never overpower them. The Guide explains why: prophecy flows from God first into a person's reasoning mind, and a mind that hasn't been trained has nowhere to hold it. Second, character. A person ruled by appetite, by greed, by the hunger for honor, is pulled too many ways to receive anything. So the work on character from his Eight Chapters, the middle way, isn't a separate subject. It's part of the same preparation. Third, imagination, the surprising one. Prophecy then flows into the imagination, he says, which is why prophets see visions, parables and dreams, not lectures. A philosopher with a strong mind but a weak imagination might understand deeply and still not be a prophet. And imagination is fragile: sadness and anger shut it down. That's how he reads Elisha: angered, he needed the music to bring back joy and calm before prophecy could come. Fourth, the limit. Does all this preparation guarantee prophecy? No. Even a fully prepared person may not receive it, Maimonides holds, if God withholds it. Preparation doesn't force the gift. It makes a person able to hold it. For him, that's the line between a vessel and a demand.
screen: `A TRAINED MIND.` · `A STEADY CHARACTER.` · `A LIVELY IMAGINATION.` · `READY IS NOT GUARANTEED.` · then, large: `PREPARE THE VESSEL.`

segments.voice: Check in on the three things Maimonides names: is your mind rested or scattered, is your character pulled by irritation, wanting or worry, is there room in you for a picture or a song? Pick the one that needs the most care, and let one small kindness toward it come to mind: a page of real reading, a grudge set down, or a piece of music, the way Elisha asked.

Prophecy needs preparation. Maimonides' teaching that prophecy comes only to someone with a trained mind, a steady character and a strong imagination, and even then only as God gives it. Today's word.
Your line: prepare the vessel. Mind, character and imagination, made ready for whatever is given. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews who study Maimonides read his account of prophecy in the Laws of the Foundations of the Torah, chapter seven, and in the second part of the Guide. Tradition holds that prophecy has ceased, so the teaching is studied as a picture of human readiness.
